name: MoE-CORE: Coordinated Expert Offloading and Residency for Memory-Constrained MoE Inference
problem: Routed experts live in host memory because the device cannot hold the pool, and the two phases want opposite fetches. Prefill activates a broad union of experts across many tokens, so a per-expert cache thrashes. Decode activates only top-k per step, so a fetch that starts after the gate sits on the critical path, and a uniform per-layer cache quota leaves the same layers under-covered on every workload.
mechanism: Keep two physically disjoint device regions. Prefill uses two buffers, each sized to one full MoE layer, and swaps them: while layer l+1 computes, the released buffer loads every expert of layer l+2. The switch to full-layer staging happens when the prefill token count reaches floor(K_l / k_l), the resident slot count divided by the routing fanout; smaller prefills stay selective. Decode keeps a per-layer expert cache inside a fixed byte budget. Slot counts are not uniform: an offline replay of hit-rate curves moves slots in steps of delta-K from layers whose hit rate stays above the median and barely drops when shrunk, to layers at least tau_low below the median whose hit rate rises the most when grown. Cache contents start from a domain profile, a request hint naming the domain, filled with the K_l experts of highest mean router score on that domain's profiling set. During decode a routing-history score evicts: recent selection count over a window W, an EMA of selections, the current router score, and age since last selection, each normalized across the layer and combined with nonnegative weights. A miss is not waited on. Before layer l+1's real hidden state exists, the original router of layer l+1 is evaluated on layer l's hidden state, and the runtime prefetches only as many of the top predicted non-resident experts as the overlap window can hide: floor of (remaining compute of layer l plus attention of layer l+1, minus launch overhead, times H2D bandwidth, divided by expert bytes), further capped by free slots. An optional approximate path, off in the main numbers, substitutes a resident unselected expert for a low-score miss whose score is within alpha of the rank-(k+1) boundary, keeping the missed expert's routing coefficient. High-score misses still take the exact host-to-device copy.
speedup_reported: Authors' own numbers, batch size 1, Ascend 950PR with 128 GB physical NPU memory, a 150 GB host-memory limit, and an 84 GB NPU-memory cap. Models are DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A8 (uniform decode cache of 84 expert slots per layer; the nonuniform allocation uses 78 slots on most layers and 120 on layers 7, 9, 19, 31, and 37) and GLM-5.2-W4A8C8 (28 slots per layer). 200 requests per dataset, output cap 1K tokens for MoE-CORE and load-on-demand, 128 tokens for the vLLM prefetch baseline. AES and MTP are off in Table 1. Mean TPOT versus load-on-demand on DeepSeek: 38.0 vs 66.5 ms (GSM8K), 42.1 vs 62.9 (AIME 2026), 44.8 vs 62.1 (HumanEval), 41.5 vs 64.1 (MMLU), 40.3 vs 70.6 (LongBench v2), which the paper states as 1.39-1.75x. GLM mean TPOT falls from 229.1-244.8 ms to 206.6-220.5 ms. Prefetch depth on DeepSeek/GSM8K: 42.6 ms with none, 36.0 ms at one expert (15.5% lower), 35.9 ms at two, 36.5 ms at three. Removing the history-aware eviction raises that TPOT from 36.0 to 46.8 ms (30%). Domain profiles and the nonuniform slot allocation each move it by about 1%. AES raises effective expert availability from 92.43% to 99.972% but increases TPOT from 36.0 to 37.7 ms at batch 1. With AES on, batch 2, and MTP depth 2, TPOT is 21.5 ms.
notes: VENUE: the abs page has no conference comment and a Crossref title query on 2026-10-18 returned nothing, so venue is arxiv-preprint. The author list on the abs page names Dan Li twice; this record lists him once. Affiliations are not stated on the abs page. WHAT TRANSFERS to a hand-written stack that already streams routed experts from host RAM while attention and shared experts stay resident: (1) size the prefill staging buffer to one full expert layer, not to the union of a token's top-k, and overlap layer l+2's copy with layer l+1's compute, switching to that path only once the token count reaches floor(resident slots / top-k) — below that, selective residency moves fewer bytes; (2) do not split a fixed decode-cache byte budget evenly per layer, because the same layers are the hit-rate troughs on every workload they measured (layers 4 and 7 bottom-ten on all five, and seven layers strict local troughs on all five, at 84 slots on DeepSeek-V4-Flash-W4A8), and move slots only when the profiled hit-rate curve says the receiver gains more than the donor loses; (3) prefetch by running the real next-layer router on the current hidden state, and cap the copy at the experts the overlap window can actually hide — one expert captured 15.5% of TPOT (42.6 to 36.0 ms) and the second bought 0.1 ms while the third raised TPOT to 36.5 ms because three expert copies no longer fit under the remaining compute; (4) evict on router score plus a short and a long selection history, not LRU, which is the 30% TPOT gap (36.0 vs 46.8 ms) in their ablation, while the domain profile and the nonuniform quota are each about a 1% effect once that eviction is in place; (5) if a miss is still outstanding, a resident expert within a small score band of the top-k boundary can stand in and keep the missed expert's routing weight, which took effective availability from 92.43% to 99.972% but cost 1.7 ms of TPOT (36.0 to 37.7) at batch 1, so it is a tail-latency tool, not a throughput one. WHAT DOES NOT TRANSFER: the headline gap against vLLM prefetch (38-45 ms vs 1269 ms TPOT on DeepSeek, 207-221 vs 5942 ms on GLM) is not a kernel result. That baseline stages complete expert layers and was capped at 128 output tokens against 1K for the others, and the paper itself says a single layer's compute cannot hide a full-layer transfer during decode. The honest comparison is load-on-demand at the same 1K cap: 1.39-1.75x on DeepSeek and roughly 10% on GLM, where the larger experts leave only 28 resident slots. All of it is one Ascend 950PR under an 84 GB cap, not a PCIe GPU, and the paper does not jointly schedule the KV cache, so a long context that shrinks the expert region is unmeasured. No code is linked.
